This site is built in honour of Edward N. Luttwak. It is not his work and he has not seen it; it is an attempt to look at the whole world, every state at once, with the lamp he built.

This atlas reads the world through Edward N. Luttwak's idea of grand strategy. Not because he is always right, but because his grid forces the questions that a map of flags leaves out: what does each actor want, with what, against what, and where do its own moves turn against it.
Strategy: The Logic of War and Peace

Luttwak stacks conflict in levels that interact but do not sum: the technical, the tactical, the operational, the theatre strategy, and above them all grand strategy, where military force meets diplomacy, economics, alliances and persuasion, and where a state's whole external conduct can be read as one design. This atlas lives on the top level only. It does not model battles or armies; it models what states and state-like actors want, the means they use across the four domains (diplomatic, informational, military, economic), what constrains them, and how they see each other.
From the lamp to the data

Each actor with a full card carries: objectives, ranked; means by domain; constraints; paradoxes; and a short reading, the only free prose. Every claim has a source with its tier (official document, research, quality press, other) and a confidence grade: A an official document or two independent sources, B one good source, C press or our own inference, always shown.

It is not a forecast and not a verdict. It is a situation map: a dated, sourced, revisable statement of where everyone stands, built region by region, with the datasets (UN votes, memberships, recognitions) as the floor and researched cards as the reading. Where a card says less than you expected, it is because the sources did not hold.
The Grand Strategy of the Roman Empire

Strategy: The Logic of War and Peace (⟨n⟩ revised ⟨n⟩) is the centre. In ordinary life linear logic rules: the shorter road is better, the stronger tool works best, more of a good thing is better. In any contest between conscious adversaries that logic fails, because the other side thinks and reacts. The bad road may be the good road because it is unguarded; the weapon that works invites the countermeasure that makes it useless; surprise is bought only with costs that would be absurd against an inert obstacle. The same logic has a temporal form, the culminating point: every success contains the seed of its reversal, the advancing army lengthens its own supply lines, the victorious power frightens the neutrals into a coalition, the sanction that bites teaches the target to do without. Pushed past that point, victory turns into defeat without any mistake having been made.

The book's second structure is vertical. Conflict runs on levels that interact but do not add up: technical, tactical, operational, theatre, and above them all grand strategy, where force meets diplomacy, economics, alliances, intelligence and persuasion. Success at one level can be undone at a higher one; strategy works when the levels are in harmony. Across all of them Luttwak distinguishes two styles: attrition, which wears the adversary down by superior resources and needs no understanding of him, and relational manoeuvre, which aims at his specific weaknesses and can win cheaply but fails badly when the reading is wrong. Great powers drift toward attrition; small states must manoeuvre. That is why, in this atlas, the cards of small states read as bets on usefulness and alignment, and the paradoxes of the great powers are about the coalitions their weight provokes.

The Grand Strategy of the Roman Empire (⟨n⟩) reads four centuries of frontier policy as three successive systems: the hegemonic empire of the Julio-Claudians, ruling through client kings and a mobile army that rarely needed to fight; the preclusive frontier of the Antonines, with its fortified lines and legions spread along them; and the defence in depth of the late empire, which conceded ground and held strongpoints behind it. The same empire, with roughly the same forces, chose different ways of converting force into security as its enemies changed. The Grand Strategy of the Byzantine Empire (⟨n⟩) describes how the eastern half survived a further thousand years with far less: by avoiding decisive battle, buying and dividing enemies, using intelligence, religion and ceremony as instruments, fighting to exhaust rather than annihilate, and treating every enemy as a possible future ally. The Grand Strategy of the Soviet Union (⟨n⟩) applied the same reading to a living adversary.

Two essays carried the logic beyond war. "From Geopolitics to Geo-Economics" (⟨n⟩) argued that with the superpower rivalry fading, states would pursue adversarial aims through economic means, subsidies, trade rules, control of technology, with the grammar of commerce but the logic of conflict: that is the logic of the dependency layer in this atlas, where gas contracts, pipelines, loans, arms and remittances are read as instruments rather than markets. "Toward Post-Heroic Warfare" (⟨n⟩) observed that advanced societies with small families will not accept casualties, so their wars become distant, aerial, delegated. "Give War a Chance" (⟨n⟩) drew the harder conclusion that an outside intervention which freezes a war before either side is exhausted often prolongs the conflict it means to stop, which is why "frozen" disputes are so prominent on these maps.

A seam is an actor pulled two ways: it is an ally of two actors that are rivals or adversaries of each other. In Luttwak's grammar the seam between an opponent and its allies is where relational manoeuvre aims, and where an alliance is tested first.
Hedging · ally of one, partner of the other

The lightest tier. A buffer is a partner of both of two actors that are rivals of each other, allied with neither: it belongs to neither and deals with both. Luttwak's Roman grand strategy kept such states between the empire and its enemies on purpose, cheap to hold and useful to both sides as long as they stayed between. The seam is the ally torn; the buffer is the partner that profits from the quarrel until it is forced to choose.

A client is an actor that leans on another more than it is leaned on: it grades the other higher than the other grades it. Luttwak's name for the arrangement is the client system of the early Roman empire, where the patron buys security cheaply because the client's loyalty exceeds the patron's commitment.
Two allies who differ only in warmth: one reads ally, the other reluctant ally. Not a client system, since both commit; the reluctant side is Luttwak's costly ally, the one that must be paid to stay.

Three conditions, all of them in the build: both readings must be hand-written at confidence A or B (provisional reciprocals and treaty-floor stances never count, so a pair appears only when both cards exist); at least one side must be an alliance (ally or reluctant ally), because a lean between two partners is a mood, not a client system; and the lean must be positive, so each pair appears once, from the client's side. Two further guards (⟨n⟩ Oct): two allies who differ only in warmth, one reading ally and the other reluctant ally, are not a client system but a tepid alliance, listed apart below; and a patron must carry at least half the weight of its client, weight being measured for now by how many cards read each actor, so that a great power never appears as the client of a small one. The last column reads the client's bond: loyal if kin or affinity, bought if none or grievance, since a bought client holds only while the patron pays.

A fault is a relationship whose deep level contradicts its surface: the bond says one thing, the posture another. Luttwak's rule is that strategy works only when its levels are in harmony; a relationship resting on a fault is the one that breaks first. Two kinds matter. A feud is kin graded rival or adversary, the quarrel inside the family, the most intense because closeness multiplies the points of contact. A Byzantine alliance is an open wound graded ally: the Byzantine maxim that every enemy is a possible ally, and the alliance that holds over the wound because it must.

Each stance carries a posture (today) and a bond (what would survive a change of government). A feud is bond kin with posture rival or adversary; a Byzantine alliance is bond grievance with posture ally or reluctant ally. A fault written by both sides of a pair is mutual; written by one side only, it says who feels it. The tendency reads the trend against the kind: a warming feud is healing, a cooling one deepening; a cooling Byzantine alliance is tearing. Only hand-written stances of confidence A or B count. Kin graded reluctant ally or reluctant partner is not a fault but a warning, strained, shown only in the ledger under the map. ⟨n⟩ faults so far, from ⟨n⟩ cards.

Where the world is moving. Every posture carries a trend, warming, stable or cooling, and the trends are the first derivative of the map: not where the relationships stand but where they are going. Luttwak's frame is the culminating point: every success carries the seed of its own reversal, and the moment a relationship turns is the moment that matters. An ally that cools is the culminating point of an alliance, the protection that has begun to cost; a rival that warms is a rivalry past its useful peak, turning into détente.
Drift · where each actor is going

Each movement is weighted by what it moves with: an ally or an adversary counts ⟨n⟩ a reluctant ally or a rival ⟨n⟩ a partner ⟨n⟩ a reluctant partner or a neutral ⟨n⟩: each step doubles, so a movement with an ally weighs eight times one with a neutral. Drift is the weighted warming minus the weighted cooling, divided by the weight of everything the actor has read: +⟨n⟩ would be an actor whose every relationship warms, −⟨n⟩ one whose every relationship cools. A state that warms with three partners moves less than one that cools with a single ally.

The level below grand strategy in Luttwak's ladder: the theatre, where geography and several actors' forces add up, and where the readings on these pages become acute. Seventeen theatres, kept by hand; an actor may sit in more than one. The heat of a theatre is computed from what the atlas has read between its members: declared hostility, seams, feuds, claimed territory and movements with stakes.

Heat is the sum of the weights between the members of a theatre, divided by the number of possible pairs, so a small dense theatre is not outweighed by a large one; ⟨n⟩ is the hottest theatre today, the others are scaled to it. Theatres whose members have few cards yet read cold for lack of data, not for peace: the card count says how far each one is written.

On the map each theatre is a zone, a circle of hand-set radius around the theatre's centre, lit in proportion to its heat; the countries inside are not coloured, because the heat belongs to the ground where the forces meet, not to the actors who send them. Click a zone to outline its members; click it again to return to the world. For every pair of members of a theatre the build adds: adversary ⟨n⟩ rival ⟨n⟩ claimed territory ⟨n⟩ a reluctant ally or reluctant partner ⟨n⟩ an ally cooling or a rival warming ⟨n⟩; for every feud inside the theatre ⟨n⟩; for every seam whose three actors are inside it ⟨n⟩ Adversaries weigh very high, rivals high, reluctant postures low. Only hand-written stances of confidence A or B count. The sum is divided by the number of possible pairs among the members, and the result is scaled so that the hottest theatre reads ⟨n⟩ The list of theatres and their members is kept by hand in data/theatres.yaml; organisations are never members. On the map the members of every theatre are lit with its heat, the hottest on top; click a country to see the hottest theatre it sits in, click the lit theatre again to return to the world, or click a theatre below to light it alone.

The enemies of my enemies. Luttwak's reading of Byzantium, in The Grand Strategy of the Byzantine Empire, is that the empire outlived Rome by a thousand years because it rarely fought the enemy in front of it: it found the enemy behind him, the Khazars behind the Avars, the Pechenegs behind the Rus, and paid him. For every actor and every enemy it reads, the build finds who else reads that enemy as hostile and whether the flank is already recruited, still open, or false, the enemy of my enemy being my enemy too. This page shows the heaviest open ones: the Byzantine move not yet made, where both the actor and the flank carry weight.

For every actor A and every X that A grades rival or adversary, the build takes every Z that also grades X rival or adversary (hand-written stances of confidence A or B; organisations never count, only those who move). Z is recruited if A or Z already reads the other as ally, reluctant ally or partner, or if a treaty or a de facto alignment binds them; false if either reads the other as rival or adversary; open otherwise, which is the flank nobody has worked. An enemy with no enemies at all leaves A alone in front of it. The index counts open flanks: many open flanks are cheap options, none means the move is spent or the actor is alone.

The logic of conflict in the grammar of commerce. In ⟨n⟩ Luttwak wrote that with the great wars over, states would carry their rivalries into the economy, with capital for firepower, market penetration for garrisons and research for armament: geo-economics. The atlas keeps a thousand dependency rows with a number in them, energy, trade, debt, investment, arms, troops. This page is the first cut of the lever: for every pair of actors of which at least one reads the other as rival or adversary, what still binds them materially. The gas a bloc buys from the power it sanctions, the market a rival cannot do without, the ground an enemy holds. Heaviest pairs first (the two weights multiplied, so a pair counts when both sides matter); one line per lever, from the card that wrote it, cut to its first sentence: the full row is in the dossier.

Luttwak's second rule for Byzantium, in The Grand Strategy of the Byzantine Empire: gather intelligence on the other and his mentality, and monitor his movements continuously. Constantinople kept an office for it, the Bureau of Barbarians, which read every envoy and every rumour from beyond the border. This page is the atlas's monitor: every week, the events that GDELT codes from the world's news are counted per country and set against the country's own four-week average. A country is surging when it makes a multiple of its normal, whatever its size; it is burning when the conflict in its news runs above its normal. The loud, who make the most news every week, are listed apart so they do not hide the rest.

The source is the GDELT Project, which has coded the world's news into events since ⟨n⟩: for every event the two actors with their country codes, the kind of act on a scale from cooperation to conflict, and the number of articles that carried it. The atlas downloads one file a day, the last seven days plus four weeks before them, and counts for every country the events it was party to.

What it is not: it measures the attention of English-language and major-language media, not what happened. A hurricane and a coup read alike until the conflict share tells them apart; the francophone Sahel and the Pacific read quiet for lack of coverage; a surge may be a summit or a scandal. It is a pointer, kept apart from the cards: the weekly update starts its searches from the surging and the burning, and nothing enters a card from here without a source read by a person. Nothing on this page is a reading of the atlas.

Grand Strategy is a situation map of the world: for every state and state-like actor, what it wants, with what means, against which constraints, and how it sees everyone else. The reading grid is Edward N. Luttwak's idea of grand strategy, and the site is built in his honour.

Each actor with a full card carries its objectives ranked, its means by domain (diplomatic, informational, military, economic), its constraints, its paradoxes (the places where its own moves turn against it) and a short reading. Every claim has a source with a tier (official document, research, quality press, other) and a confidence grade: A an official document or two independent sources, B one good source, C press or our own inference, always shown.

How one actor sees another is recorded on two axes. The posture is the relationship today, on a closed scale: own territory, claimed but not controlled, ally, reluctant ally, partner, reluctant partner, neutral, rival, adversary. "Adversary" is kept for mortal enemies, where the other's existence or regime is the problem; nearly all bad relationships are rivalries. The grade follows the structural position, never the rhetoric of a communiqué: two members of the same alliance with open friction are reluctant allies, not rivals. The bond is what lies under the posture and would survive a change of government: kin, affinity, none, or grievance. On the map the posture is the colour of the outline and of the light inside a country; the bond is a band inside the border; a dashed band marks a partner aligned with the actor as a bloc, without a treaty.

Under the postures sit the relation rows, in four layers: objectives (what an actor wants from another), alignments (treaties, memberships, recognitions), dependencies (energy, trade, debt, arms, remittances, with numbers) and actions (dated events: votes, sanctions, visits, exercises). The datasets are the floor: memberships from Wikidata and official lists, recognition tables from Wikipedia with their citations, every recorded vote of the UN General Assembly since ⟨n⟩ from the UN Digital Library. The cards are the reading on top of that floor. A lighter floor still is the Watch: every week the events GDELT codes from the world's news are counted per country and set against the country's own four-week average, Luttwak's Byzantine rule of monitoring the other continuously; attention, not truth, kept apart from the cards, and a pointer for where the next update should look.

A client is an actor that leans on another more than it is leaned on: it grades the other higher than the other grades it. Luttwak's name for the arrangement is the client system of the early Roman empire, described in The Grand Strategy of the Roman Empire: the hegemonic empire of the Julio-Claudians ruled through client kings whose loyalty exceeded Rome's commitment to them, which is why it was cheap. The Clients page measures the lean of every pair the atlas has read from both sides, in steps on the posture scale; the higher-grading side is the client, the other the patron. A client bound by kin or affinity is loyal; one bound by nothing, or by a grievance, is bought, and holds as long as the patron pays. The tepid ally, graded "ally" by its patron and answering "partner", is the costly kind, the one Rome subsidised. In the ledger under the map the lean column shows, for each counterpart, who leans on whom.

A fault is a relationship whose deep level contradicts its surface. The frame is Luttwak's structure of levels: in Strategy success at one level can be undone at a higher one, and a strategy works only when its levels are in harmony. Here the levels are two: the bond, which would survive a change of government, and the posture of today. Two contradictions matter. The feud is kin graded rival or adversary, the quarrel inside the family, which Luttwak counts as the most intense of rivalries because closeness multiplies the points of contact. The Byzantine alliance is a grievance graded ally: the maxim from The Grand Strategy of the Byzantine Empire that every enemy is a possible ally, and the alliance that holds over an open wound because it must. The Faults page lists both, says whether each is felt by one side or both, and reads its trend as healing or tearing; on the map a fault shows as a bond band that contradicts the colour of its outline.

Every posture carries a trend, warming, stable or cooling, and the trends are the first derivative of the map: not where the relationships stand but where they are going. The frame is Luttwak's culminating point, the moment at which a success begins to produce its own reversal. The Currents page reads the trends two ways. The alarms: allies that are cooling, which is the culminating point of an alliance, the protection that has begun to cost, and rivals that are warming, the rivalry past its useful peak. And two measures per actor: drift, which way its world is going, and turbulence, how much of it is moving. Each build keeps a snapshot of every grade, so the page can also say what changed since the last one. On the map, in the posture lens, a warming relationship pulses and a cooling one flickers, like phosphor brightening or dying.

Below grand strategy in Luttwak's ladder of levels sits the theatre, where geography and several actors' forces add up and where strategy is actually conducted. The atlas keeps a hand list of seventeen theatres, from the Western Balkans to the Southern Cone, and computes for each a heat from what it has read between the members: declared hostility, seams, feuds, claimed territory and movements with stakes, divided by the number of possible pairs so that a small dense theatre is not outweighed by a large one. The Theatres page has its own map, lit by heat, and the list of what makes each theatre hot. A theatre whose members have few cards reads cold for lack of data, not for peace.

The enemies of my enemies. Luttwak reads Byzantium's survival as the refusal to fight the enemy in front when the enemy behind him could be found and paid: the Khazars against the Avars, the Pechenegs against the Rus. The Flanks page runs that search for every actor: for each enemy it reads, who else reads that enemy as hostile, and whether that flank is already recruited (a written friendship, a treaty or a de facto alignment), false (the enemy of my enemy is my enemy too) or still open, the move nobody has made. The page shows the heaviest open flanks, where both the actor and the flank carry weight; an actor whose enemies have no enemies stands alone.

In ⟨n⟩ Luttwak gave a name to the form rivalry would take once the great wars were over: geo-economics, the logic of conflict in the grammar of commerce, capital in place of firepower, market penetration in place of garrisons. The atlas keeps the material dependencies between actors with their numbers: energy, trade, debt, investment, arms, troops. The Levers page lists every such dependency between two actors of which one reads the other as rival or adversary, the handle one side holds over the other, or that both hold. It is a first cut; the direction of each lever is in the row's summary, not yet in a field of its own.

The data lives in plain files, one per actor, separate from the site, and is versioned in the open: the whole history of every grade is in the repository. Cards are researched and drafted by language-model agents working from a shared brief and the atlas's own rules, then reread by a stronger model that checks objectives, paradoxes and every posture grade against the sources and against the neighbouring cards; the owner samples the result. A new card's grades retroact on the cards already written as provisional reciprocals, flagged as such until written from the other side. Nothing is embedded in the site: it renders the data as it stands on the day of the last build, and the stamp in the top bar says which day that was. The Data page counts all of it: actors, readings, rows, sources by tier, the datasets and when they were taken, what the build derives, and what it has cost.

It is not a forecast and not a verdict. Where a card says less than you expected, it is because the sources did not hold. Where a posture surprises you, open the dossier: the note under each grade says why it was read that way, and the footnote says who said so.

Who made it, how it is built, and how it runs. The terms are explained under About; the counts are on Data.

The truth is a folder of plain text. Every actor has three YAML files: the card (objectives, means, constraints, paradoxes, reading, each with sources and a confidence grade), its stances (how it reads every other actor: grade, trend, bond, since, last verified, note, sources) and its relations (rows in four layers: objectives, alignments, dependencies, actions). Vocabularies are closed: nine grades, four bonds, three trends, a fixed list of relation types. A stub is an actor with the first file only, a node without a card. Beside the cards sit the datasets, taken by small scripts from one source each and never edited by hand: states and memberships from Wikidata and the organisations' lists, recognition tables from Wikipedia, every recorded vote of the UN General Assembly from the UN Digital Library, GDP, military spending and population from the World Bank, borders from Wikidata.

One Python script, the build, turns that folder into the site. It validates every file and refuses to write on any error: an unknown id, a grade outside the vocabulary, a date that does not parse, a claim without a source. It then derives what no card states: treaty allies from the memberships, a provisional mirror for every reading not yet answered from the other side, and the computed pages, seams, buffers, clients, faults, gatherings, encirclement, flanks, levers, currents, theatres, each by a rule written in the ontology. It keeps a snapshot of every grade, so the next build can say what moved. It writes one JSON for the site and one bundle per actor, so any other front end could read a state on its own.

Everything is versioned in git, in the open: the whole history of every grade is in the repository, and a change to the ontology is made only with a journal entry. The atlas is updated on the editor's call, never on a calendar. When he calls, the datasets are refreshed first (they cost nothing), then the dates the cards said to watch, then a short regional scan that lists the cards an event touched, then those cards only: a dated row added, a trend or a grade moved when a source says so, never a rewrite. Between calls, single news items go in as one dated row each.
